summary: Jordan lies in West Asia, bordering Israel, Syria, Iraq and Saudi Arabia, and has the ancient city of Petra and the Dead Sea; it has taken in large numbers of Palestinian and Syrian refugees.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: After the Arab conquest in the 7th century, the inhabitants of this region gradually converted to Islam, with Sunni Islam as the mainstream. Most of Jordan's population are Bedouin tribes and Palestinian refugees who poured in after the wars of 1948 and 1967, both predominantly Sunni. The Hashemite royal family claims descent from the Prophet and treats moderate Islam as part of the national identity.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: Jordan's Christians are one of the oldest Christian communities in the Arab world, dating back to before the rise of Islam, mostly Greek Orthodox and concentrated in Madaba, Salt, Fuheis and Amman. Because of emigration to the West and a lower birth rate, their share has fallen from about 10 percent in the early 20th century to about 3 percent now, but they have guaranteed seats in parliament and influence in business and education.

ranking.name: Other
ranking.description: This includes a small number of Shias, Druze, some groups among the Circassians and Chechens who fled the Russian Empire from the Caucasus in the late 19th century (most of whom are still Sunni), and other faiths that came with refugees and foreign workers.

religion.background: The Jordan River is where Jesus was baptized in the Bible, and Jordan has early Christian sites such as Mount Nebo and Madaba; Christianity was already spreading here in the 1st–4th centuries. After the Arab Muslim conquest in the 7th century, Islam gradually became the majority religion, and from the 16th century the Ottoman Empire ruled the region. In 1921 the Hashemite family, backed by Britain, founded the Emirate of Transjordan, which became independent in 1946; the royal family claims to be descendants of the Prophet Muhammad, and its legitimacy to rule is closely tied to Islam. Jordan's constitution makes Islam the state religion, but guarantees Christian communities freedom of worship and reserves seats in parliament.

ranking.name: Arabic (Jordanian dialect)
ranking.description: Arabic has been the language of the inhabitants since the Islamic conquest in the 7th century, and the constitution makes it the official language. The Jordanian dialect belongs to Levantine Arabic; because of the large influx of Palestinian refugees, the accent in cities such as Amman is very close to Palestinian dialects, while villages and Bedouin tribes speak more traditional dialects.

ranking.name: Circassian (Adyghe)
ranking.description: From the 1860s, Circassians who were forced to leave after the Russian Empire conquered the Caucasus were resettled by the Ottoman Empire and settled around Amman; in fact they were among the early founders of the modern city of Amman. Their Adyghe language has gradually declined through assimilation with Arabic, but the Circassians still serve in the royal guard and have guaranteed seats in parliament.

language.history: In antiquity the region of Jordan used Nabataean (the language of the builders of Petra), Aramaic and Greek, and after the Islamic conquest in the 7th century Arabic became the main language. The Jordanian dialect belongs to Levantine Arabic, with urban dialects close to Palestinian dialects, while Bedouin tribes keep a more conservative dialect. Modern Standard Arabic is used in formal settings and in writing. The English left from the British Mandate era (1921–1946) has had a profound influence, and today English is widely used in education and business.

ranking.name: Mansaf
ranking.description: Lamb is stewed in a sour, salty sauce made from fermented dried yogurt (jameed), laid over thin bread and rice, sprinkled with almonds and pine nuts, and traditionally eaten by hand.
ranking.history: Mansaf comes from the nomadic diet of Jordan's Bedouin tribes: sheep are the main property, and jameed is sheep's milk fermented and dried so that it keeps in the desert. In the early 20th century rice replaced the earlier crushed wheat, giving today's form. It is regarded as Jordan's national dish and appears at weddings, funerals, festivals and tribal reconciliation ceremonies; eating together with the host around a big platter signifies generosity and trust.

ranking.name: Maqluba
ranking.description: Meat, fried eggplant or cauliflower and other vegetables are layered with rice in a pot and cooked, and when served the whole pot is flipped upside down onto a large platter. After flipping it shows handsome layers and is often eaten with yogurt or salad.
ranking.history: Maqluba means "upside down" in Arabic, the name coming from the act of flipping it over when served. Some sources trace similar dishes to 13th-century Baghdadi cookbooks, but the modern version is popular mainly in Palestine and Jordan. In Jordan it is closely tied to the food culture of the many Palestinian immigrants and is often made for Friday family meals; it is a common joyful scene for the whole family to clap when it is flipped.

ranking.name: Musakhan
ranking.description: Roast chicken is placed on taboon bread and covered with plenty of onions sauteed with sumac and olive oil, then sprinkled with pine nuts. It tastes tangy and fragrant, and is often rolled up and cut into small pieces to eat as a snack.
ranking.history: Musakhan originated in rural northern Palestine and is traditionally made each autumn when the olives are harvested and the first fresh oil is pressed, to celebrate the harvest and taste the new oil. After the wars of 1948 and 1967, large numbers of Palestinians moved to Jordan and brought the dish into Jordan's daily diet. It is regarded by many as the Palestinian national dish and is also extremely common in Jordan.

ranking.name: Falafel
ranking.description: Ground chickpeas with coriander, parsley and spices are shaped into small balls and deep-fried, and tucked into bread with tahini and pickles. The outside is crisp and the inside green and fluffy, and it is a common inexpensive breakfast in Jordan.
ranking.history: Falafel is generally thought to have originated in Egypt (where fava beans are mostly used), and later spread throughout the Levant using chickpeas instead. In Jordan it is the most common commoner's breakfast and late-night snack, and the long-established snack shop Hashem in downtown Amman (founded in the 1950s) has been visited even by members of the royal family. Being cheap, vegetarian and filling has made it a national food eaten by all classes.

ranking.name: Knafeh
ranking.description: Fine vermicelli-like pastry threads or a coarse semolina dough wrap stretchy white cheese, baked until golden, then drenched in syrup and sprinkled with crushed pistachios. The crust is crisp and the cheese inside stretches in strings, and it is best eaten hot.
ranking.history: The origin of knafeh is much disputed; one account holds that it comes from Egypt and the Levant in the medieval Fatimid or Mamluk period, and Nablus in Palestine is the most famous for cheese knafeh. Palestinian immigrants brought it to Jordan, and long lines often form in front of famous sweet shops in Amman. It is especially popular after the nightly fast-breaking during Ramadan, and is also a dessert for weddings and for celebrating exam success.
